column1:
User says: 'VPN shows Connected, but I can’t open any internal apps.' What is the BEST first step?

A. Check routing and DNS with route print + ipconfig /all
B. Disable Windows Firewall
C. Flush DNS cache only
D. Reinstall VPN client
column2:
Correct Answer: A. Check routing and DNS with route print + ipconfig /all

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
route print

What it checks:
DNS servers/suffix and whether internal routes exist

Why it works:
Most VPN failures are routing/DNS, not the client install

Success indicates:
Internal routes present and DNS points internal; proceed to reachability tests

Failure indicates:
No internal routes or DNS still public

Common pitfall:
Jumping to reinstall without checking evidence

column1:
VPN connected. User can browse the internet, but internal names (intranet.company.local) do not resolve. What is MOST likely?

A. Split tunnel is enabled
B. DHCP lease expired
C. DNS is not set to internal DNS over VPN
D. Gateway is down
column2:
Correct Answer: C. DNS is not set to internal DNS over VPN

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
nslookup intranet.company.local

What it checks:
Which DNS server answers and whether internal suffix is present

Why it works:
Internal names require internal DNS; public DNS won’t know them

Success indicates:
nslookup shows internal DNS server and returns internal IP

Failure indicates:
nslookup times out or returns NXDOMAIN from public DNS

Common pitfall:
Testing ping before confirming name resolution source

column1:
VPN connected. Internal names resolve, but ping to the resolved internal IP fails. What does this suggest?

A. User typed the name wrong
B. DNS is working but routing/ACL is blocking traffic
C. VPN is not connected
D. Browser cache issue
column2:
Correct Answer: B. DNS is working but routing/ACL is blocking traffic

Command(s) to run:
nslookup <internal-name>
ping <resolved-internal-ip>
tracert <resolved-internal-ip>

What it checks:
Name resolution vs reachability and hop where traffic stops

Why it works:
DNS can succeed even if routing/firewall blocks connectivity

Success indicates:
tracert reaches internal network and ping succeeds after fix

Failure indicates:
tracert stops or times out before destination

Common pitfall:
Assuming DNS success means access is fine

column1:
User reports: 'With VPN on, internet stops working, but internal apps work.' What is MOST likely?

A. Full tunnel VPN with restricted internet access/policy
B. Split tunnel misconfigured
C. DNS cache issue
D. Local NIC failure
column2:
Correct Answer: A. Full tunnel VPN with restricted internet access/policy

Command(s) to run:
route print
ipconfig /all
ping 8.8.8.8

What it checks:
Whether default route points to VPN and whether external reachability exists

Why it works:
Full tunnel sends internet traffic into VPN; policy may block it

Success indicates:
Default route via VPN and internal works; internet restored after policy/proxy fix

Failure indicates:
No external reachability while VPN is default route

Common pitfall:
Assuming it’s 'DNS' without checking routes

column1:
User reports: 'With VPN on, internal apps fail, but internet works normally.' What is MOST likely?

A. Split tunnel missing internal routes
B. Full tunnel enabled
C. Browser issue
D. Antivirus update
column2:
Correct Answer: A. Split tunnel missing internal routes

Command(s) to run:
route print
ping <internal-ip>

What it checks:
Presence of internal subnet routes via VPN

Why it works:
Split tunnel requires explicit routes to internal networks

Success indicates:
Routes present and internal IP reachable after fix

Failure indicates:
No internal routes; ping fails

Common pitfall:
Only checking DNS when the IP itself is unreachable

column1:
VPN connected. User can reach internal IPs over VPN but cannot access internal websites by name. What is MOST likely?

A. VPN disconnected
B. DNS issue (internal DNS not in use)
C. Wrong subnet mask
D. Routing issue
column2:
Correct Answer: B. DNS issue (internal DNS not in use)

Command(s) to run:
ping <internal-ip>
nslookup intranet.company.local
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
Reachability vs name resolution and DNS source

Why it works:
If IP works but names fail, DNS is the separator

Success indicates:
nslookup uses internal DNS and resolves; browser works

Failure indicates:
nslookup fails or uses public DNS

Common pitfall:
Treating every problem as routing

column1:
User reports: 'VPN connected but I only can access one internal app; others fail.' What is a likely cause?

A. ACL/firewall allowing some subnets/ports only
B. DNS server down
C. Corrupt profile
D. DHCP exhausted
column2:
Correct Answer: A. ACL/firewall allowing some subnets/ports only

Command(s) to run:
tracert <app1-ip>
tracert <app2-ip>
route print

What it checks:
Whether different destinations follow different paths or are blocked

Why it works:
Policies can allow limited access while blocking others

Success indicates:
Blocked path fixed or ACL updated

Failure indicates:
Tracert stops for failing apps

Common pitfall:
Assuming one app working means full access

column1:
VPN connected. User’s DNS server remains set to 8.8.8.8 and internal names fail. What is the BEST next action?

A. Disable IPv6
B. Reimage
C. Restart Print Spooler
D. Confirm VPN is pushing DNS and reconnect; escalate if not
column2:
Correct Answer: D. Confirm VPN is pushing DNS and reconnect; escalate if not

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
Disconnect/reconnect VPN
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
Whether the VPN client pushes DNS settings on connect

Why it works:
Many VPNs assign DNS on connect; if it doesn’t, internal resolution breaks

Success indicates:
DNS changes to internal server after reconnect

Failure indicates:
DNS stays public; needs VPN profile/policy fix

Common pitfall:
Only flushing DNS cache instead of fixing DNS source

column1:
User’s VPN is full tunnel. They can’t reach a printer on their local home network while connected. Why?

A. Local LAN traffic is routed into VPN (no local access)
B. DHCP lease expired
C. DNS issue
D. Printer driver issue
column2:
Correct Answer: A. Local LAN traffic is routed into VPN (no local access)

Command(s) to run:
route print
ping <printer-ip> (VPN on/off)

What it checks:
Whether local subnet routes are overridden by VPN default route

Why it works:
Full tunnel can block local LAN access by design

Success indicates:
Local LAN access returns when split/local routes enabled

Failure indicates:
Printer unreachable only when VPN is on

Common pitfall:
Troubleshooting printer drivers instead of routing

column1:
VPN connected but internal access fails. route print shows no routes for internal subnets. What does this indicate?

A. Route injection/profile issue (split tunnel)
B. DHCP outage
C. DNS cache issue
D. User typed wrong password
column2:
Correct Answer: A. Route injection/profile issue (split tunnel)

Command(s) to run:
route print
ping <internal-ip>

What it checks:
Whether internal subnet routes exist via VPN interface

Why it works:
If routes aren’t installed, traffic never enters tunnel

Success indicates:
Internal routes appear after profile fix; access restored

Failure indicates:
No routes; internal unreachable

Common pitfall:
Assuming 'Connected' means routing is installed

column1:
VPN works from home but not from public Wi-Fi. What’s a realistic first hypothesis?

A. Captive portal or restricted network blocking VPN
B. Wrong VLAN at office
C. DHCP exhaustion
D. DNS suffix missing
column2:
Correct Answer: A. Captive portal or restricted network blocking VPN

Command(s) to run:
Confirm internet access in browser
ping 8.8.8.8
Try VPN again

What it checks:
Whether the network allows required VPN traffic

Why it works:
Public Wi-Fi can block VPN until portal accepted

Success indicates:
VPN connects after portal/network change

Failure indicates:
VPN consistently blocked on that Wi-Fi

Common pitfall:
Spending time on client config when network blocks VPN

column1:
VPN connected. Internal names resolve, but only some users can access a specific subnet. What should you do?

A. Disable Windows Firewall
B. Compare route print across users and escalate with evidence
C. Flush DNS
D. Reinstall VPN client
column2:
Correct Answer: B. Compare route print across users and escalate with evidence

Command(s) to run:
route print (affected)
route print (working)
Document user/group

What it checks:
Policy/route differences per user/group

Why it works:
VPN policies can be assigned by group

Success indicates:
Routes added and access restored

Failure indicates:
Subnet missing routes for some users

Common pitfall:
Escalating without comparison data

column1:
User says: 'VPN connected, but my PC shows no internet.' Internal apps work. What should you check FIRST?

A. Disable Bluetooth
B. Reimage PC
C. Full tunnel policy and external reachability
D. Reset password
column2:
Correct Answer: C. Full tunnel policy and external reachability

Command(s) to run:
route print
ping 8.8.8.8
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
Whether default route is VPN and whether external access is allowed

Why it works:
Some full-tunnel profiles intentionally block internet

Success indicates:
Internet works if policy allows or split tunnel enabled

Failure indicates:
No external reachability by design/policy

Common pitfall:
Treating the tray icon as definitive

column1:
User can access internal by FQDN but short names (server01) fail. What is MOST likely?

A. DNS suffix/search list missing
B. VPN disconnected
C. Routing issue
D. DHCP lease expired
column2:
Correct Answer: A. DNS suffix/search list missing

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
nslookup server01
nslookup server01.company.local

What it checks:
Suffix search list behavior

Why it works:
Missing suffix breaks short-name resolution even if FQDN works

Success indicates:
Suffix corrected; short names resolve

Failure indicates:
Short names fail until suffix fixed

Common pitfall:
Assuming short-name failure is routing

column1:
VPN connected. Internet works, DNS resolves internal names, but an internal web app returns Access Denied only for this user. What is MOST likely?

A. DHCP scope issue
B. Application/identity authorization issue
C. Routing issue
D. DNS issue
column2:
Correct Answer: B. Application/identity authorization issue

Command(s) to run:
Confirm others can access
Document exact error; escalate to app/identity team

What it checks:
Authorization vs connectivity

Why it works:
If reachability is fine but app denies, it’s usually permissions

Success indicates:
Access restored after permissions fix

Failure indicates:
Connectivity remains fine; access denied persists

Common pitfall:
Continuing network troubleshooting after confirming reachability

column1:
User says: 'VPN connected and internal works, but speed is terrible.' What’s a good first check?

A. Change password
B. Flush DNS
C. Measure latency/path to internal resource
D. Disable DHCP
column2:
Correct Answer: C. Measure latency/path to internal resource

Command(s) to run:
ping <internal-ip> -n 10
tracert <internal-ip>

What it checks:
Latency and hop count over VPN path

Why it works:
Long paths/hairpin routing cause slowness

Success indicates:
Latency improves after route/ISP fix

Failure indicates:
High latency persists

Common pitfall:
Assuming the server is slow without measuring

column1:
VPN connected. User can resolve internal names, but ping to internal gateway works while internal servers fail. What’s likely?

A. DNS issue
B. Wrong password
C. VPN disconnected
D. ACL/routing beyond the gateway
column2:
Correct Answer: D. ACL/routing beyond the gateway

Command(s) to run:
ping <internal-gateway>
tracert <internal-server-ip>

What it checks:
Where traffic stops beyond first hop

Why it works:
Gateway reachability doesn’t guarantee end-to-end routing

Success indicates:
Tracert reaches servers after policy fix

Failure indicates:
Stops after gateway

Common pitfall:
Stopping at first-hop success

column1:
User loses VPN connection every few minutes. What is a reasonable FIRST check?

A. Check packet loss/stability to VPN gateway
B. Disable DHCP
C. Edit hosts file
D. Change DNS suffix
column2:
Correct Answer: A. Check packet loss/stability to VPN gateway

Command(s) to run:
ping <vpn-gateway> -n 20
tracert <vpn-gateway>

What it checks:
Stability/packet loss on the path

Why it works:
Unstable connectivity drops tunnels regardless of config

Success indicates:
Low loss after network fix; VPN stable

Failure indicates:
High loss correlates with drops

Common pitfall:
Assuming credential/auth issue without checking stability

column1:
VPN connected. User can ping internal IP but SMB (file share) fails. What should you do next?

A. Gather evidence for port/policy block and escalate
B. Reinstall Windows
C. Disable UAC
D. Flush DNS
column2:
Correct Answer: A. Gather evidence for port/policy block and escalate

Command(s) to run:
ping <server-ip>
tracert <server-ip>
Document that SMB/445 fails

What it checks:
Reachability vs service/policy restrictions

Why it works:
ICMP may work while SMB is blocked by ACL

Success indicates:
SMB works after policy update

Failure indicates:
Ping works but SMB fails

Common pitfall:
Concluding network is fine because ping works

column1:
User can connect to VPN on Wi-Fi but not on wired at home. What should you compare first?

A. Disable firewall
B. Adapter IP/DNS/routes (Wi-Fi vs Ethernet)
C. Reinstall VPN client
D. Reset password
column2:
Correct Answer: B. Adapter IP/DNS/routes (Wi-Fi vs Ethernet)

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (Wi-Fi)
ipconfig /all (Ethernet)
route print

What it checks:
Adapter-level differences and route behavior

Why it works:
Different adapters can have different DNS/MTU/firewall behavior

Success indicates:
VPN works after fixing wired network settings

Failure indicates:
VPN fails only on wired

Common pitfall:
Assuming the client is broken

column1:
VPN connected. User says: 'Internal apps fail, but only when I’m on home Wi-Fi; mobile hotspot works.' Most likely?

A. VPN account locked
B. Company DNS down
C. Windows corruption
D. Home network issue (DNS/MTU/firewall)
column2:
Correct Answer: D. Home network issue (DNS/MTU/firewall)

Command(s) to run:
ping <vpn-gateway>
tracert <vpn-gateway>
Test hotspot vs Wi-Fi

What it checks:
Path differences between networks

Why it works:
Hotspot success points to local router/Wi-Fi restrictions

Success indicates:
VPN works on Wi-Fi after router config fix

Failure indicates:
VPN fails only on home Wi-Fi

Common pitfall:
Reinstalling VPN client when hotspot proves it works

column1:
VPN connected. route print shows default route via VPN. User says cloud apps (Teams/Outlook) behave poorly. What is MOST likely?

A. Printer spooler
B. Full tunnel policy impacting cloud traffic
C. DNS A record issue
D. DHCP lease time
column2:
Correct Answer: B. Full tunnel policy impacting cloud traffic

Command(s) to run:
route print
ping 8.8.8.8

What it checks:
Whether the VPN is full tunnel (default route via VPN)

Why it works:
Full tunnel/filtering can degrade cloud app performance

Success indicates:
Cloud apps stabilize after split/full adjustment

Failure indicates:
Cloud apps fail when VPN default route enforced

Common pitfall:
Assuming it’s an app issue without checking tunneling mode

column1:
VPN connected. User has internal DNS and internal routes, but internal access still fails. What is the best next step?

A. Flush DNS
B. Test reachability to internal IP and use tracert to find where it stops
C. Reinstall client
D. Disable antivirus
column2:
Correct Answer: B. Test reachability to internal IP and use tracert to find where it stops

Command(s) to run:
ping <internal-ip>
tracert <internal-ip>

What it checks:
Where traffic is blocked after config looks correct

Why it works:
If routes/DNS look right, confirm path and block point

Success indicates:
Tracert reaches destination after fix

Failure indicates:
Tracert stops at a hop or times out

Common pitfall:
Stopping at config checks without testing reachability

column1:
User says: 'VPN connects, then prompts for credentials repeatedly.' What’s a plausible cause?

A. DNS suffix issue
B. MFA/conditional access or saved credentials mismatch
C. Subnet mask wrong
D. DHCP exhausted
column2:
Correct Answer: B. MFA/conditional access or saved credentials mismatch

Command(s) to run:
Confirm account works (web sign-in if available)
Retry credentials and note MFA prompts

What it checks:
Auth vs networking separation

Why it works:
Repeated prompts often indicate auth/token/MFA issues

Success indicates:
Auth succeeds; VPN stable

Failure indicates:
Prompts continue; escalate to identity team with details

Common pitfall:
Assuming it’s routing when it’s auth

column1:
User can access internal sites by name but RDP to internal hosts fails. What’s likely?

A. VPN disconnected
B. DNS issue
C. Wrong subnet mask
D. Policy/port differences (web allowed, RDP blocked)
column2:
Correct Answer: D. Policy/port differences (web allowed, RDP blocked)

Command(s) to run:
ping <rdp-target-ip>
tracert <rdp-target-ip>

What it checks:
Reachability and likely policy blocks by service

Why it works:
Different services may be restricted by policy

Success indicates:
RDP allowed after policy change

Failure indicates:
Reachable but service blocked

Common pitfall:
Treating all internal access as identical
